**The Imjin War (1592–1598)** | Aspect | Details | |--------|---------| | **Full name** | Imjin War (임진왜란) – “Imjin” refers to the Chinese lunar year 1592 (the year of the Tiger). | | **Belligerents** | • **Japan** – led by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, seeking to conquer Korea and expand into China.
• **Joseon Korea** – a tributary state of Ming China, defended by the Joseon army and navy.
• **Ming China** – intervened in 1597 to support Joseon. | | **Timeline** | • **April 1592** – Japanese forces land on the Korean coast (Busan).
• **Late 1592** – Japanese advance northward, capturing Seoul and the capital city of Gyeongju.
• **Early 1593** – Korean–Ming forces regroup; naval victories at the Battle of Hansan Island (1592) and the Battle of Myeongnyang (1597).
• **1597–1598** – Ming forces launch a major counter‑offensive; Japanese forces retreat to the southern coast.
• **July 1598** – Japanese forces withdraw from Korea after the death of Hideyoshi. | | **Key Battles** | • **Battle of Hansan Island** – Admiral Yi Sun-sin’s torpedo‑armed “turtle ships” decimated Japanese supply lines.
• **Battle of Myeongnyang** – Yi Sun-sin’s 12‑ship fleet defeated a Japanese fleet of 133 ships with only 12 vessels.
• **Battle of Noryang** – final naval engagement; Yi Sun-sin died in the battle. | | **Causes** | • Hideyoshi’s ambition to conquer China via Korea.
• Korea’s strategic position as a gateway to the Chinese mainland.
• Japan’s desire to secure trade routes and acquire resources. | | **Consequences** | • Massive destruction in Korea: cities, temples, and infrastructure were devastated.
• Loss of life: estimates range from 200,000–400,000 Korean civilians and soldiers, and 30,000–50,000 Japanese troops.
• Strengthened Korean naval tactics and the reputation of Admiral Yi Sun-sin.
• Decline of the Japanese military after Hideyoshi’s death.
• Long‑term diplomatic strain between Korea and Japan, influencing relations for centuries. | | **Historical Significance** | • Demonstrated the effectiveness of naval power and innovative ship design.
• Highlighted the importance of logistics and supply lines in warfare.
• Served as a cautionary tale about overreaching imperial ambitions. | **Quick Takeaway:** The Imjin War was a brutal conflict where Japan attempted to invade Korea, but Korean and Ming Chinese forces ultimately repelled the invasion, largely thanks to Admiral Yi Sun‑sin’s naval victories.
